Each tool type is accompanied by links to sample studies and systematic reviews.

---

## 1. AI Chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT)
**Function:**  
These tools use large language models to simulate conversation, provide step-by-step problem solving, answer math-related questions, clarify concepts, and give explanations tailored to student queries. Some can generate full solutions or hints for math problems on-demand.

- Example features: Interactive Q&A, Socratic dialog, personalized explanations, math anxiety reduction support.
- Studies:
  - Wardat et al. (2023). Case study of ChatGPT for teaching and learning mathematics. [PDF](https://www.ejmste.com/download/chatgpt-a-revolutionary-tool-for-teaching-and-learning-mathematics-13272.pdf)
  - Lo (2023). Rapid review of ChatGPT's educational potential across subjects, including math. [PDF](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/13/4/410/pdf?version=1681825504)
  - Deng & Yu (2023). Meta-analysis of chatbot technology effects in education. [PDF](https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/15/4/2940/pdf?version=1676433939)

---

## 2. Generative AI-powered Tutoring Systems (Adaptive/Intelligent Tutors)
**Function:**  
These systems use AI to present math problems, assess student responses, provide immediate feedback, and adapt instructional content. Some embed generative AI to create novel problems or explanations, simulate a Socratic tutor, and track student progress.

- Example features: Stepwise feedback, adaptive scaffolding, dynamic question generation, learning-by-teaching setups (e.g., “teachable agents”).
- Studies:
  - Xing et al. (2025). Design-based research on a generative AI-powered teachable agent for secondary mathematics. [Abstract & Full Text](http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/bjet.13586)
  - Li et al. (2025). Systematic review of AI tool use in K-12 mathematics education. [PDF](https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2025.3585784)

---

## 3. Automated Problem Generators
**Function:**  
These tools use generative models to create novel, level-appropriate math problems (including word problems, multiple-choice, or open-ended types), and sometimes supply worked solutions. They can generate differentiated sets for individualized practice or classroom use.

- Example features: On-demand problem banks, personalized assignments, teacher-controlled parameters.
- Studies:
  - Reviewed within Li et al. (2025). [PDF: See Section on “Automated Problem Generation Tools”](https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2025.3585784)  
  - Referenced in Tang et al. (2025) – Generative AI as a teaching assistant in the classroom. [Abstract & Full Text](http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/jcal.70027)

---

## 4. Adaptive Feedback and Assessment Platforms
**Function:**  
These systems use generative AI to analyze student responses, identify misconceptions, and deliver tailored feedback, either in real time or asynchronously. Some merge analytics with generative models to refine explanations or hints as students work.

- Example features: Personalized feedback, error-specific hints, data-driven formative assessment.
- Studies:
  - Heung Yue Yim & Su (2024). Scoping review details types of AI learning tools and feedback in K-12 education. [PDF](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9.pdf)
  - Tang et al. (2025). Teacher-supervised generative AI as a classroom assistant. [Abstract & Full Text](http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/jcal.70027)

---

## 5. "Teachable Agents" Using Generative AI
**Function:**  
Students "teach" a virtual character powered by generative AI, which asks questions, points out errors, and displays learning behaviors based on student input. This approach leverages the pedagogical strategy of "learning by teaching."

- Features: Simulated student agent, reciprocal questioning, generative explanations.
- Study:
  - Xing et al. (2025). Generative AI teachable agent for middle school math [Abstract & Full Text](http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/bjet.13586)

---

## 6. Integrated Platforms (Multi-tool Ecosystems)
**Function:**  
Some recent platforms combine several of the above features (chatbot help, adaptive feedback, problem generation, and tutoring) within a single ecosystem, optimized for math classrooms.

- Studies:
  - Li et al. (2025). Systematic review documents integrated AI tools in K-12 math.
- Coverage: [PDF](https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2025.3585784)

---

---

### Key Educational Settings and Contexts

#### 1. Classroom-Based Implementation

- **General/Classroom Environments**: The vast majority of GenAI tool deployments in mathematics have occurred within standard classroom settings. These include both typical math classrooms and some with special contextual features (e.g., urban schools, resource/support classrooms).
    - *Example*: Xing et al. (2025, Rung 2–3, Design-Based Research, Middle School, n not specified) report on the iterative development and classroom deployment of a GenAI-powered teachable agent (“MathBot”) that supports learning-by-teaching in middle school mathematics. The study documents integration directly into daily lessons, with observation and iterative co-design with teachers.  
      - Citation: Xing, W., Song, Y., Li, C., Liu, Z., Zhu, W., & Oh, H. (2025). Development of a Generative AI-Powered Teachable Agent for Middle School Mathematics Learning: A Design-Based Research Study. [ERIC EJ1480025](http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/bjet.13586)  
    - *Example*: Tang et al. (2025, Mixed Methods, Rung 2) examine GenAI as a teaching assistant within classrooms in a study involving adolescents, highlighting the importance of teacher supervision when integrating AI into day-to-day math instruction.
      - Citation: Tang, Q., Deng, W., Huang, Y., Wang, S., & Zhang, H. (2025). Can Generative Artificial Intelligence Be a Good Teaching Assistant? [ERIC EJ1474776](http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/jcal.70027)

#### 2. Special Education / Resource Rooms

- **Special Education**: GenAI tools, such as ChatGPT, have been adapted for specialized environments, particularly to support instructional planning, adapt lesson materials, and reduce teacher workload in middle school special education/resource rooms.
    - *Example*: Walter (2025, Qualitative Case Reflection, Rung 2) describes practical use in a middle school special education classroom (grades 6–8), assisting both teachers and students mainly in classroom and resource room settings, with some use for creating personalized content and simplifying texts.
      - Citation: Walter, A. (2025). Enhancing Special Education with Generative AI: Suggestions from Our Practice. [ERIC EJ1483969](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1483969)

#### 3. Teacher Support/Professional Learning

- **Support for Teachers and Curriculum Adaptation**: GenAI is often deployed to assist teachers in planning math lessons and scaffolding curriculum within the classroom environment, especially in urban public school districts.
    - *Example*: Malik et al. (2024, EdWorkingPaper, Rung 2–3) report on LLMs (like ChatGPT) used as a curriculum design aid for middle school math teachers to create tailored scaffolds in diverse classrooms.
      - Citation: Malik, R., Abdi, D., Wang, R., & Demszky, D. (2024). Scaffolding Middle-School Mathematics Curricula with Large Language Models. [ERIC ED660105](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED660105)

#### 4. Online and Blended Learning

- **Blended/Hybrid Approaches**: Some studies report use of GenAI in blended learning scenarios, with students interacting with GenAI agents both in and out of the classroom (e.g., for homework help, remote learning activities). However, these approaches are less common in the peer-reviewed literature.
    - *Systematic Review Insight*: Borah & Borah (2024, Systematic Review, Rung 3) indicate that online/remote implementations (e.g., via AI-based intelligent tutoring systems) have been deployed, but most studies focus on settings tied to formal school environments, rather than purely after-school or informal learning.
      - Citation: Borah, P. & Borah, A. (2024). A Review of Use of Artificial Intelligence in Teaching and Learning of Mathematics. [OpenAlex](https://doi.org/10.71097/ijsat.v15.i4.1190)

#### 5. High School Settings

- **Less Prevalent but Emerging**: Relatively fewer peer-reviewed studies detail GenAI math tool deployment specifically at the high school level between 2020–2026; most focus on middle school environments. Where present, these are typically in general math classes or as personalized online support.
    - *Example*: Chen et al. (2025, Quantitative, High School, Rung 2–3) investigate the relationship between math anxiety and GenAI tool usage for problem-solving in high school classroom settings.
      - Citation: Chen, F., Chen, J., & Xu, Y. (2025). The More Anxious, the More Dependent? The Impact of Math Anxiety on AI-Assisted Problem-Solving. [ERIC EJ1477358](http://dx.doi.org/10.1002/pits.23500)

#### 6. Notable Absences

- **After-School, Out-of-School, and Informal Settings**: There is very limited peer-reviewed research on the use of GenAI for math learning in after-school programs, extracurricular clubs, community centers, or other informal settings as of early 2026. Most examined implementations are closely tied to school day curricula and teachers.

---

### School Types & Demographic Contexts

- **School Types**: Most reported studies involve public schools (including urban districts), with some special education and international settings, but with very little detail available on private, charter, or rural school contexts.
- **Demographic Details**: Some studies mention diverse or multilingual classrooms (especially in urban districts), but very few provide extensive subgroup analyses.
